children.text: A Chinese community cemetery of about 54 hectares in Santa Cruz, northern Manila, where Chinese Filipinos have been buried since the late 19th century. House-like mausoleums line its streets, Chong Hock Tong Temple and anti-Japanese war memorials still stand, and entry on foot is reported to be free.

The Manila Chinese Cemetery is a burial ground of about 54 hectares in the Santa Cruz district in the north of the City of Manila. It was set aside for non-Catholic Chinese who could not be buried in Catholic cemeteries during the Spanish colonial period, and together with La Loma Cemetery next door it counts among the oldest cemeteries in Manila. It is said to have begun when Lim Ong (林旺), a leader (gobernadorcillo) of the Chinese community of Binondo, bought land on the hill of La Loma and donated it; records put this at around
or
. In

more land was bought from a Dominican hacienda to enlarge the cemetery, and the memorial temple Chong Hock Tong was built. Today it is owned and managed by a Chinese charity, the Philippine-Chinese Charitable Association (PCCA).

What made this place famous is its mausoleums, which are closer to houses than to graves. Family mausoleums line the paved roads like a residential neighborhood, and those of wealthy families come with kitchens, flush toilets, sinks with hot and cold water, air conditioning and even chandeliers. That is how it earned nicknames such as "Millionaires' Row" and "Little Beverly Hills." At the same time there are humble resting places for those of lesser means, such as the niches in the perimeter wall and the Kong Tek Tong hall, a reminder that the gap between rich and poor continues after death.

For travelers who love architecture, it is a museum without a roof. Southern Fujian swallowtail roofs and pagoda-shaped mausoleums stand on the same street as Art Deco, Neo-Gothic and even a mausoleum modeled on an Egyptian temple, while tombs with a cross on top of a Chinese roof and altars that bring Taoist, Buddhist and Catholic images together tell the story of Chinese Filipino (Chinoy) life over nearly 150 years. According to a study of the hometowns carved on the gravestones, most of those buried here came from southern Fujian (Minnan) and most of the rest from Guangdong. During World War II the Japanese army used the cemetery as an execution ground, and several anti-Japanese war memorials stand here.

It is still a working cemetery where funerals and grave visits go on. It is not set up as a tourist attraction, so there are hardly any signs or shops, but it suits travelers interested in history, architecture and Chinese Filipino culture. How Chinese Filipinos live is covered in the
Binondo Chinatown
entry; this entry covers where they rest after they have gone. Compare it with the
Manila American Cemetery
, where white crosses stand in rows on a lawn, and the difference in the cultures behind the two cemeteries becomes clear.

Mausoleums are most densely packed along the main road from the South Gate toward Chong Hock Tong Temple and the side streets beside it. Walk along looking from the road at mausoleums with marble columns, iron-grille doors, portraits of the deceased and even balconies. The roads carry the names of people tied to the cemetery, such as Lim Ong Road, Consul Gen. Young Rd. and Mabini Road.
Built in
, Chong Hock Tong (崇福堂) was the oldest Chinese memorial temple in Manila until it was torn down on
March 15, 2015
on the grounds of termite damage, setting off a controversy over the loss of heritage. The present building was rebuilt in stone after the old design and unveiled on
. Taoist, Buddhist and Christian services are all held here, and images from several religions share the altar.
In the shade of a huge tree in front of Chong Hock Tong stands a bust of Carlos Palanca (Chinese name Tan Quien Sien). Born in
, he was a merchant who led the Chinese community of Manila in the late 19th century and is credited with funding the construction of the temple.
With its red columns and yellow walls, the Martyrs Hall (Liat See Tong, 烈士堂) was built in the
early 1950s
to honor 10 leaders of the Chinese community executed by the Japanese army. Their portraits hang side by side behind the grille.

blocks.title: Anti-Japanese war memorials and the Consul General Young Memorial

children.text: The black stone Philippine Chinese Anti-Japanese War Memorial, erected in

, and the memorial hall behind it honor the resistance of Chinese guerrillas. The memorial to Clarence Kuangson Young, consul general of the Republic of China, who turned down offers to evacuate, stayed, was seized by the Japanese army and was executed with seven consulate staff on
April 17, 1942
, was put up by the Chinese community in
Before dawn on
August 2, 1968

, the magnitude 7.3 Casiguran earthquake brought down Ruby Tower, a six-story apartment building in Santa Cruz, killing more than 250 people, most of them Chinese Filipino residents. The memorial behind the Martyrs Hall was built in
; photographs of the victims are mounted beneath its three pillars joined by a ring.
Apolinario Mabini, known as the "Brains of the Revolution," was buried in this cemetery after he died of cholera on
. His remains were later moved by way of another cemetery and reburied in
in his hometown of Tanauan, Batangas, and a small pyramid monument and a historical marker installed in
remain on the original spot.

blocks.title: Turtle-back tombs and the Ma Mon Luk mausoleum

children.text: Fujian-style turtle-back tombs with a rounded mound are actually rare in this cemetery, so they are worth looking out for. Beside the mausoleums are small altars to the earth god Houtu (后土) and burners for paper money. The mausoleum of Ma Mon Luk (
), the restaurant owner who popularized mami noodles, also stands here with its stone lions.
Get off at Abad Santos Station on LRT Line 1 and walk about
10 minutes
to the South Gate. Tell the guard at the entrance that you have come to look around, then go in.
Walk along the main road from the South Gate, comparing mausoleums in different styles.

See Chong Hock Tong Temple and the Carlos Palanca Memorial. A map of the cemetery hangs in the administration office behind the temple; ask permission and take a photo of it to make finding your way easier.
See the Martyrs Hall and then the Ruby Tower Memorial behind it.
Look around the Anti-Japanese War Memorial and its memorial hall, and the Consul General Young Memorial.
See the pyramid at Mabini's first grave and the turtle-back tombs, then head back out through the South Gate.
Go down to Binondo by LRT or Grab for lunch.
Old Manila Walks, well known for its Manila walking tours, runs a Chinese Cemetery tour. The group meets in front of Chong Hock Tong Temple and spends about
2 hours
going around turtle-back tombs, Art Deco plots and multi-story mausoleums while hearing the history of the Chinese community. It costs
per person (
on weekends and holidays) and must be booked; some months have no scheduled dates, so check the dates on the official site first.
If you come without a booking, you can also ask one of the cemetery caretakers near the South Gate to show you around. Bargain for a rate of about
for
1 hour
, and settle the total and the length of the tour before setting off.
A good order is to walk the cemetery in the cooler morning, then ride LRT Line 1 about
10 minutes
from Abad Santos Station down to Carriedo Station and have lunch in
Binondo Chinatown
. In the afternoon, walk to
Quiapo Church
or take a Grab over to
Intramuros

southeast of the station, roughly a
10-minute
walk.

Enter "Manila Chinese Cemetery South Gate" as the destination. The South Gate is at the end of Felix Huertas Street, near Aurora Boulevard.
Normally you can drive into the cemetery, but parking space is limited. Around All Saints' Day on
November 1
, vehicles are barred from entering and part of nearby Aurora Boulevard is closed, so use public transport.
The cemetery stretches about
1.2 km
from north to south, and the main sights are clustered along the way from the South Gate to Chong Hock Tong Temple in the old northwestern section, so you can see them on foot in
2–3 hours
. Guidebooks say bicycles can be rented for about
an hour, but check on the spot whether this is available.
Since you will be walking on paved roads with little shade, the weather matters a great deal.
December–February
is relatively cool and dry and best for walking, while in
March–May
midday temperatures climb to around
, so it is better to walk only in the early morning.
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and typhoons affect the area in
July–September
The cemetery is at its busiest twice a year. On Qingming, the Chinese tomb-sweeping festival (around
April 4–5
), and on All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day in the Philippines (
November 1–2

), families gather at their mausoleums, lay out food, burn incense and paper money and spend the day there. It is a chance to see these customs, but it is private family time and comes with vehicle restrictions and crowds, so avoid it if you want a quiet walk. Even then it is far quieter than the neighboring Manila North Cemetery, which draws huge crowds.

The area around the cemetery is a mix of houses, hospitals and markets, with almost no accommodation for travelers. Most visitors stay in Binondo (about
a night), in Ermita or Malate (about
a night) or in Makati or BGC and come for half a day.

There are no restaurants or shops inside the cemetery, so bring water and eat before or after your visit. Binondo is close if you get off at Carriedo Station, five stops away on LRT Line 1. Try mami (chicken broth noodle soup) and siopao (steamed meat buns), the dishes popularized by Ma Mon Luk, whose mausoleum is in this cemetery, and the stories you heard among the tombs will carry on at the table. See the Binondo Chinatown entry for where to eat.
The gate to use is the South Gate. Map apps sometimes direct you to another gate, so set the South Gate at the end of Felix Huertas Street as your destination.
No opening hours have been officially announced. Guidebooks give
and other sources
, so it is safest to visit between
8:00 AM and 3:00 PM
. Check the latest notices.
The grounds are large and signs are few. Take a photo of the cemetery map at the administration office behind Chong Hock Tong Temple, and check your position on your phone's map app as you walk.

Taking photos with a phone is generally fine, but some visitors report being asked not to shoot video. Do not photograph the inside of mausoleums, portraits of the deceased or families holding a funeral.
Mausoleums are private family spaces. Do not go in even if the door is open, and do not touch the food, incense or flowers on the altars.
Bring water, a hat, a sun umbrella and comfortable shoes. In the rainy season you will also need a folding umbrella and mosquito repellent.

This is not a tourist facility but a private cemetery where funerals are still held. Opening hours, the gates in use and entry rules can change without notice, and vehicles and entry are restricted around All Saints' Day and Qingming. Follow the instructions of the guards at the entrance and check the latest notices.
Many sections are deserted. Keep to the main paved roads, do not go deep into narrow alleys alone, and leave before sunset.

Some people will tag along offering to guide you. Decline clearly if you do not want this, and if you do hire someone, agree on the fee and the time first. If you are asked for an entrance fee at the gate, ask for a receipt.
The way from the station to the South Gate passes through a working-class residential area and a market. Wear your bag in front and keep your phone and camera out of sight.
With so little shade, the risk of heatstroke is high at midday. Drink water often and rest in a pavilion or under a tree.
Neglected mausoleums have broken steps and railings or are slippery with moss. Do not climb on or lean against the structures.
Caretaker families also live inside the cemetery, looking after the mausoleums. Do not photograph their living spaces or the people without permission.
About

About
